<explanation>
Based on the file structure and README, Libredesk is an open source, self-hosted customer support desk built as a single binary application. It has a clearly separated backend (primarily written in Go) and a frontend built with Vue.js (using Shadcn for UI components). The project’s purpose is to manage customer conversations efficiently (with features like multi-inbox, automation, macros, SLA and more), so your diagram should capture both the high-level system components and the lower-level Go modules, as well as the rich Vue component tree on the frontend.

Here’s a step-by-step guide to creating an accurate system design diagram for Libredesk:

1. Main Components Identification:
   • Backend (Go Application): 
     - Core business logic is spread across many internal directories (e.g., internal/auth, internal/conversation, internal/automation, internal/inbox, internal/csat, internal/macro, internal/notification, internal/sla, etc.). There is also a “cmd” folder which indicates multiple entry points or commands for various functionalities such as AI, authentication, conversation, etc.
     - Database interactions are evident through many queries.sql files and database setup in the installation section.
     - Additional modules provide support for attachments, file/media handling, integrations with channels/messages, event notifications, and websockets.
     - Automation, rules evaluation, and auto-assignment further indicate business rule engines within the backend.
   • Frontend (Vue.js Application):
     - A dedicated “frontend” directory holds assets, components (many UI components, layouts, views, composables, router, and stores), and testing configurations.
     - The frontend is structured to support a dynamic user interface with modules for login, administration, conversation details, reporting, and more.
   • Database:
     - The README and the installation instructions reference a Postgres DB setup.
   • External Services:
     - Docker Compose files, a Dockerfile, and references to deployment workflows indicate containerization.
     - AI functionality and web socket communications are integrated (look at internal/ai, internal/ws).
   • Configuration & Deployment:
     - Configuration is managed through TOML files (config.sample.toml) and deployment scripts (Makefile, goreleaser config, Docker-compose) plus CI/CD workflows under .github.
  
2. Architectural Relationships and Interactions:
   • When drawing the diagram, separate the frontend and backend components.
   • Show how the frontend (Vue.js) communicates with the backend via HTTP APIs and possibly web sockets for real-time updates.
   • Represent the backend as several logical modules or services. While it’s a single binary, you can divide it into clusters (e.g., authentication, conversation management, automation, notifications, etc.) based on the internal directory structure.
   • Connect the backend to the Postgres Database. Indicate the use of SQL queries in various modules.
   • Depict integrations with external systems such as email channels (see internal/inbox/channel/email) and third-party AI providers (internal/ai).
   • Include Docker and deployment configuration as components for setup and scalability.

3. Architectural Patterns and Design Principles:
   • The project follows a modular monolith structure where functionalities (conversations, automations, roles, users, etc.) are encapsulated in dedicated packages.
   • There is a clear separation of concerns:
       - Backend business logic and core functionalities are well-organized by domain in the internal directory.
       - The frontend is structured into UI components, layouts, views, and state management (stores).
   • Communication is based on API calls (HTTP REST) and websockets.
   • The design hints at extensibility via modular internal components (for example, automation rules and customizable macros).

4. Guidelines for Tailoring Your Diagram:
   - For a full-stack application:
     • Clearly separate the frontend and backend.
     • Represent the database as a central component with arrows indicating data flow from backend modules.
     • Detail the API layer along with the websocket connection for real-time interactions.
   - Include relevant technologies: Go, Postgres, Docker, Vue.js, Shadcn UI, and any CI/CD integrations (GitHub Actions workflows, Goreleaser).
   - If needed, reference the modular monolith approach by grouping related internal modules together.

5. Diagram Element Recommendations:
   • Use clearly labeled boxes for key components:
     - Frontend (with sub-components like layouts, pages, and UI libraries)
     - Backend Modules (each major domain such as authentication, conversation, automation, notification, etc.)
     - Database (Postgres)
     - External integrations (email services, AI providers, and websockets)
     - Deployment/Infrastructure (Docker containers, CI/CD pipelines)
   • Use directional arrows to show interactions:
     - Indicate API calls from the frontend to the backend.
     - Show data flow from backend modules to the database.
     - Depict event-driven communications (via websockets or automation triggers).
   • Apply color coding or different shapes:
     - Different shapes for presentation (frontend) vs. business logic (backend) vs. data storage (database) vs. deployment scripts/infrastructure.
  
6. Additional Details and Best Practices:
   • Annotate each module with brief notes about its responsibility. For example, the “internal/automation” package handles rule evaluation and auto-assignment.
   • Include versioning aspects (e.g., configuration version, migrations under internal/migrations).
   • Since Libredesk is a single binary with multiple functions, illustrate how various commands (located in the cmd directory) call into the core engine.
   • Emphasize the separation of concerns and point out component dependencies (like how media handling interacts with file storage or S3).

By covering these details and clearly labeling every component, you’ll ensure the diagram accurately reflects the architectural design of Libredesk. This level of detail will assist any developer or architect who wants to understand the system’s internal organization and communication paths.

Happy diagramming!
</explanation>
